companions.label: PCE inflation
companions.why: The Fed's 2% target is set on this index, not the CPI. It usually runs a few tenths lower.

source.fred_title: Personal Consumption Expenditures: Chain-type Price Index

companions.label: Core PCE inflation
companions.why: The Fed's preferred measure of underlying inflation; its 2% target applies here.

source.fred_title: Personal Consumption Expenditures Excluding Food and Energy (Chain-Type Price Index)

companions.label: Core CPI (ex food and energy)
companions.why: When headline and core diverge, food or energy prices are doing the work.

source.fred_title: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items Less Food and Energy in U.S. City Average

companions.label: Headline CPI (all items)
companions.why: The all-items index, including food and energy.

source.fred_title: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items in U.S. City Average

companions.label: U-6 (incl. part-time for economic reasons and marginally attached)
companions.why: The broadest official measure of slack. Only published since 1994.

source.fred_title: Total Unemployed, Plus All Persons Marginally Attached to the Labor Force, Plus Total Employed Part Time for Economic Reasons, as a Percent of the Civilian Labor Force Plus All Persons Marginally Attached to the Labor Force (U-6)

companions.label: Prime-age (25–54) employment-to-population ratio
companions.why: Share of 25–54-year-olds with a job. Sidesteps arguments about who counts as 'looking for work'. Different scale: read it against its own level, not the unemployment rate's.

companions.label: CBO estimate of the natural rate of unemployment
companions.why: The Congressional Budget Office's estimate of the rate consistent with stable inflation. An estimate, revised over time.

companions.label: Sahm rule indicator
companions.why: 3-month average unemployment rate minus its low of the prior 12 months. A reading of 0.5 or more has coincided with the start of every recession since 1970.

companions.label: Household survey employment, change from month before
companions.why: The other monthly jobs count, from the survey of households rather than employers. Noisier, and it counts the self-employed.

companions.label: Continuing claims
companions.why: People still collecting benefits, not just newly filing. Different scale: it runs several times larger than initial claims.

companions.label: Single-family starts
companions.why: Starts of one-unit homes only. The rest of the total is apartments, which move on a different cycle.

source.fred_title: New Privately-Owned Housing Units Started: Single-Family Units

companions.label: Consumer price index
companions.why: Used to compute the price level.

source.fred_title: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items in U.S. City Average

companions.label: Average hourly earnings, change from a year ago
companions.why: Pay for production and nonsupervisory workers, about four-fifths of private employment. When this line is above inflation, typical paychecks are gaining ground.

source.fred_title: Average Hourly Earnings of Production and Nonsupervisory Employees, Total Private

companions.label: 30-year mortgage rate, monthly average
companions.why: Used to compute the mortgage spread.

source.fred_title: 30-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage Average in the United States

companions.label: 3-month average
companions.why: Smooths the month-to-month noise; the first print of any month is revised twice.

companions.label: Real Fed funds rate (minus core CPI inflation)
companions.why: The policy rate after inflation. Above zero means money costs something in real terms; below zero, policy is loose whatever the headline rate says.

companions.label: 10-year yield minus Fed funds rate
companions.why: The slope of the curve. Below zero (an inverted curve) has preceded every recession since the 1970s, usually by a year or more.

companions.label: Price level, 2019 average = 100
companions.why: The index itself rather than its growth rate: what a 2019 dollar's worth of goods costs now. Inflation is the slope of this line; the line itself does not come back down.

companions.label: Real wage growth (hourly earnings minus CPI inflation)
companions.why: Wage growth after inflation, as a simple difference. Above zero, pay is outrunning prices; below, prices are winning. Compares against headline CPI on both charts.

companions.label: Mortgage rate minus 10-year yield
companions.why: The spread lenders charge over Treasuries. Normally 1.5–2 points; wider in stress, as in 2022–24.

companions.label: Jobs added, as first reported
companions.why: The number announced on jobs day, before the two later revisions. The gap to the current line is the revision. History is still being backfilled; earlier months arrive over the next few days.

companions.label: GDP growth, advance estimate
companions.why: The first of three estimates for each quarter. Revisions of a full point are not unusual.

companions.label: Unemployment rate, as first reported
companions.why: Rarely revised by more than 0.1 point; here mainly to show that.

companions.label: Inflation, as first reported
companions.why: Seasonal factors are recalculated each February, so past months shift slightly.
